newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Blast damages Cuban tourist office in Bahamas.
newsitem.headline: Blast damages Cuban tourist office in Bahamas.

text.p: Bahamas police on Wednesday said they had asked the United States to send bomb experts to help investigate a weekend blast at a Cuban tourist office that shattered windows and damaged four other businesses in central Nassau.
The explosion at Havanatur (Bahamas) Ltd. occurred on Sunday night, several hours before a small bomb went off at the Mehia Cohiba Hotel in Havana early on Monday morning.
There were no injuries reported in connection with the blast.
Spence Finlayson, owner of Diana's Last Child Productions, which was damaged in the explosion, said he had reopened his business on Tuesday.
"It's a shock that something like that would happen in the Bahamas. I understand from the authorities that this was done by someone who knew what they were doing, not locally," he said.
Police said they did not know who was responsible or if the blast was linked to the bomb in Havana. "We're just trying to put the thing together now," said Bahamas Police Commissioner B.K. Bonamy.
"It is a matter that we are taking very seriously and which we will investigate with a fine-tooth comb," he said.

He said the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation was sending in experts to assess the situation. The Bahamas police have a standing relationship with the FBI and Interpol and the FBI's involvement comes under that relationship, he said.

The bombing on Monday in the lobby of Havana's Melia Cohiba hotel came three weeks after similar bombs damaged the lobbies of two other Havana tourist hotels, the Nacional and the Capri. Another blast was reported at the Cohiba in April.
Cuba said the bombings were organised and supplied by people in the United States, which Cuban exiles angrily denied.

Members of Alpha 66, an exile group that advocates armed struggle against Cuba's Communist government, said on Thursday in Miami that the group's "cell" in Cuba had phoned an Alpha 66 office in New Jersey and said it was responsible for the two July bombings.
Nelson Garcia, treasurer of record of Havanatur in the Bahamas, refused to comment on the incident. "Anything you want to know, call the police. They have better information than I do," he said.
